title: Marlow and Sia's Chasm Rescue
markdown:
The sky broke into pink and gold. Sunlight hit Marlow’s floorboards and then his face. Outside, a woodpecker tested the old oak as if the tree had overslept. Marlow was already up. Boots. Pack. The day had a sound to it, bright and impatient.

He grabbed the backpack that lived ready: rope, torch, a first-aid kit with the plaster peeling on one corner. Under the maps his fingers found paper that crackled. A brittle yellowed note. Whispering Chasm. Hikers lost. Air is thin.

His heart kicked. The forgotten mine adit. People in the dark. He was out of the house before the kettle had quite decided to boil.

Sia was at the school gates, wrapping a scraped knee with the kind of calm that made panic look underdressed.

“Sia.” Marlow skidded. “Hikers. Whispering Chasm. The note says the air is thin. We go now.”

Her eyes sharpened, concern first, then the medic’s sorting. “The Chasm. That place is not a dare, Marlow.”

“They need us. You’ve got the kit. I know the rock. We are a team.”

Sia’s mouth almost smiled. She had always liked his weather, even when she did not trust it. “Quick, then. Careful. Extra water. And the hard biscuits. The ones that survive being sat on.”

They filled bottles at the school tap until the packs pulled honest. Sia added the biscuits, two foil blankets, and a whistle Marlow pretended not to need. The lane out of town was already warm. Dew flashed on the verges and then gave up. A tractor coughed in a far field. Marlow talked the whole first mile: the note, the adit, a winter he had crawled the lower workings when the stream was low. Sia let him. She saved her breath for the hill.

The path gave up being a path. Trees closed, branches like fingers that had not decided to grab. Birds went from chorus to the odd remark, then to nothing. Then the hillside opened: a dark mouth in vine and stone, cool air sliding out with the smell of wet earth and old iron.

Sia stood a moment in that breath. “The woods have gone quiet here.”

Marlow lit the torch. The beam made a hard road through the gloom. Mineral glints answered like cheap stars. “Close. Watch your feet.”

Deeper, the air thickened. Footsteps, drip, drip, drip. Old pick marks in the wall, as if the hill remembered being worked and had not forgiven it. Marlow’s torch found a rusted tin, a bootlace, a place where someone had sat and ground a heel into dust. The main adit ran straight a while, then shouldered left. Water ticked in a rhythm that wanted to be a clock and was only water.

Sia checked a small monitor, frowned, checked again. “Oxygen’s falling. Faster than I like. We do not linger for the scenery.”

Marlow swept the passage. A newer scrape on the right wall, pale against the soot. “Side tunnel. Rock’s fresher. Disturbed. They may have taken it.”

They squeezed through. Packs scraped. The passage made them duck, then crawl, then duck again. Marlow’s helmet kissed stone and sang a dull note. He held up a hand.

A cry, thin as thread. Then another, weaker, as if the first had spent itself.

He wanted to shout. He did not. Sia’s look was enough. They went on, and the rock opened into a small cavern, and two figures sat huddled, pale, used up.

“We’re here,” Marlow said, and kept it smaller than the triumph in his chest. “We’ll get you out.”

The hikers lifted their heads as if the words were a rope. Sia was already kneeling, pulse, breath, the quiet inventory. “Weak. Not finished. Easy now.”

Marlow walked the walls with the torch and found a climb that tasted of clearer air. “This way. Narrow. Better than sitting still.”

They moved as one tired animal. Water first, small sips, Sia’s voice keeping the hikers from gulping themselves sick. One had a knee that would not take weight; Marlow made a sling from the rope and his own stubbornness. Sia talked them through the bad footholds the way she talked scraped knees at the gate: facts, then the next fact. Marlow tested each hold twice, which was unlike him and exactly like the note in his pack. The climb bit. A ledge crumbled to grit. He found another. The thought of moss and sky did the rest, and when the torch battery dipped he did not say so until they were on better rock.

They came out into late sun that felt almost rude. The hikers folded onto the green and took the air in greedy, ordinary gulps. Marlow and Sia stood in the light they had been hurrying toward and did not, for a minute, know what to do with their hands.

Later the first stars arrived, tentative, as if checking whether the day was finished. They sat without filling the quiet. The Chasm kept whatever it kept. The note in Marlow’s pack had gone soft at the fold from being held too often.

Sia packed the monitor away. Marlow clicked the torch off, though there was nothing left to cut. The click was a small sound. It finished something the dawn had started.

Below them the oak held the last of the woodpecker’s work. Tomorrow would come in with the same pink racket if it wanted. Tonight the hikers were breathing, and the two of them were only sitting, and that, for once, was the whole of the adventure.
characters: Marlow (an amateur caver), Sia (a school medic)
